content:
## What This Pattern Is For

Use the Generate pattern when you want the AI to create something new — a first draft, a starting structure, a set of ideas, or a piece of code you'll build on. The goal isn't to get a finished product. It's to get a useful starting point faster than you could build it from scratch.

Good examples of when to Generate:
- You need a first draft of something you've never built or written before
- You want a few options to react to instead of starting from a blank page
- You need a skeleton structure so you can focus on filling in the details
- You're brainstorming and want raw material to work from

## The Key Mindset: You're Getting a Draft, Not a Deliverable

The biggest mistake with this pattern is treating the output as finished. It isn't. AI-generated content almost always needs to be reviewed, adjusted, and adapted before it's actually yours.

This doesn't mean the output is bad — it means the process isn't over. Think of it like getting a rough draft from a collaborator: it gives you something to react to, cut, reshape, and own.

**Before you prompt:** know what you'll look for when you review the output.

**After you get the output:** don't ask "is this good?" Ask "what do I need to change to make this work for my actual situation?"

## Being Specific Prevents Generic Output

The more vague your Generate prompt, the more generic the output. The AI will make guesses about your intent and produce something that technically fits the request but doesn't quite fit *your* project.

**Vague → generic:**
> "Generate a webpage for my project."

You might get a generic layout with placeholder headings, a stock navigation bar, and filler content that has nothing to do with what your project is actually about.

**Specific → useful:**
> "Generate the HTML and CSS for a simple homepage for my school environmental club. It should have a header with the club name and a short tagline, a section listing our three upcoming events, and a footer with a contact email. Keep the styling clean and minimal — no animations. The page should look good on both desktop and mobile."

Now the AI has enough to produce something you can actually work with on the first try.

## Use Constraints to Avoid Generic Output

Constraints aren't restrictions — they're guardrails that keep the output useful. When you tell the AI what to avoid or what to stay within, it can't default to the generic answer.

Useful constraints for Generate prompts:
- **Scope:** "Only generate the function, not the full script."
- **Style:** "Keep it minimal — don't add features I didn't ask for."
- **Format:** "Give me three different options, not just one."
- **Audience:** "It needs to work for someone who has never encountered this before."
- **Technical limits:** "Use only built-in Python libraries — no external packages."

## Example Prompts

**Generating a starting structure for a coding project:**
> "Generate the skeleton for a Python text-based quiz game. It should have a function to ask a question, check the answer, and keep track of the score. Don't build the full game — just give me the structure I can fill in with my own questions and logic. Add comments explaining where I'll need to add things."

**Generating ideas to react to:**
> "I'm creating a five-minute presentation on the environmental impact of fast fashion for my environmental science class. Generate five different ways I could open the presentation to grab the audience's attention. For each idea, give it a short name and one sentence explaining why it would be effective. I'll pick one to develop."

**Generating a starting point for a data project:**
> "Generate a set of 20 realistic but made-up data entries I can use to test my program. Each entry should have a student name, a grade level (9–12), a subject, and a test score (50–100). Format it as a Python list of dictionaries. I'll replace it with real data later — I just need something to work with while I build."

**Generating a draft piece of writing:**
> "Generate a first draft of a letter to my school's administration proposing a new student recycling program. Include why it matters, what the program would look like, and a call to action. Keep the tone respectful and persuasive. I'll rewrite and personalize it — I just need a structure to react to."

## What to Do After You Generate

- **Read the whole output** before you use any of it
- **Compare it to your actual goal** — does it match what you described, or did the AI make assumptions?
- **Identify what to keep, what to change, and what to cut** — treat it like editing a draft, not accepting a submission
- **Don't be afraid to generate again** with a more specific prompt if the first result missed the mark

Generating once and moving on skips the most important step. The value of this pattern comes from using the output as fuel for your own thinking — not replacing it.
